title: A two-week, station-specific timetable trial is the committee’s chosen test for missed night‑bus transfers
description: Rather than implementing system-wide changes or immediately altering signage, the committee will run a narrowly scoped, measurable experiment: move the last night‑bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks (only at that station) and log outcomes before deciding whether to keep the change.
audience: Municipal transport officials, transit planners, local reporters covering transport policy
rationale: This idea highlights a concrete, evidence‑based decision: a short, local operational trial with predefined measurement (dispatcher logs of completed transfers and onward delays). It is useful to readers who follow how public agencies test fixes, because it shows a limited, testable approach that preserves options while collecting data.
evidence: Source states committee's trial: 'move the last night bus departure at Harbor Junction five minutes later for two weeks, without changing departures at other stations.' It adds that 'Dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays before the committee decides whether to retain the change.' The source also notes signs were discussed but set aside for this trial.

title: Most missed transfers were caused by a timetable mismatch, not train lateness
description: Staff logs show 17 missed transfers in four weeks; in 14 cases the bus had already left when a train that was arriving 'within its published time' reached the platform, while the remaining three missed transfers were associated with train delays—pointing to a schedule alignment problem at Harbor Junction.
audience: Transit operations teams, schedule planners, transport analysts
rationale: This is a focused diagnostic insight grounded in the committee's data. It directs attention to the relative timing of published train arrivals and bus departures—an operational problem that can be addressed through timetable alignment or targeted trials.
evidence: Source: 'Staff observed 17 missed transfers in the four weeks they logged. In 14 of those cases, the bus had already left when a train arriving within its published time reached the platform. Logs for the other three show train delays.'

title: The initial review was narrowly scoped and did not test schedule changes—so a follow-up experiment was required
description: The committee’s review covered Harbor Junction only and explicitly 'did not test whether a schedule change would improve transfers.' The planned two‑week, five‑minute timetable adjustment is therefore a direct response to that gap in the original review.
audience: Local policymakers, oversight committees, civic journalists
rationale: Readers interested in public accountability and process will value understanding the limits of the original review and why a targeted experiment is the next logical step. The idea is about process and the incremental approach to problem solving.
evidence: Source states: 'The review covers Harbor Junction only. It did not test whether a schedule change would improve transfers.' The planned trial (moving the last night bus departure five minutes later for two weeks) follows that finding.

title: Success will be judged by dispatcher‑logged completed transfers and onward delays
description: The committee will rely on dispatcher logs as the primary data source to evaluate the two‑week timetable test—specifically recording which transfers are completed and any resultant delays on onward services—before deciding whether to keep the change.
audience: Transit performance analysts, auditors, operations managers
rationale: Metric choice determines what the experiment can prove. Emphasizing the concrete metrics—completed transfers and onward delays—helps readers evaluate whether the trial is likely to produce actionable evidence.
evidence: Source: 'Dispatchers will log completed transfers and onward delays before the committee decides whether to retain the change.' The public briefing guidance also says it 'should explain ... what the temporary timetable test will measure.'

title: Signage was considered as an alternative but was set aside for the timetable trial
description: The committee discussed improving signs to address missed transfers but decided to defer that option and run the timetable test first, leaving signage improvements as a potential later action.
audience: Communications and wayfinding specialists, transit advocates, local community groups
rationale: This idea surfaces a visible alternative that the committee explicitly considered and postponed. It matters to readers interested in passenger information and low‑cost fixes, because it flags that an informational approach was on the table but not chosen for the initial test.
evidence: Source statement: 'Better signs were discussed, but the committee set them aside for this trial.'
